claim: The escape trajectory (ET) of prey plays a major role in avoiding predation.
source: The escape trajectory (ET) of prey – measured as the angle relative to the predator's approach path – plays a major role in avoiding predation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational premise of the study.

claim: Previous geometric models predict a single ET.
source: Previous geometric models predict a single ET; however, many species show highly variable ETs with multiple preferred directions.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to previous work in the field.

claim: Many species show highly variable ETs with multiple preferred directions.
source: Previous geometric models predict a single ET; however, many species show highly variable ETs with multiple preferred directions.
evidence: This is stated as an empirical observation contrasting with previous models.

claim: The novel geometric model incorporates the time required for prey to turn and the predator's position at the end of its attack.
source: Here, we constructed a novel geometric model that incorporates the time required for prey to turn and the predator's position at the end of its attack.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach of the study.

claim: The optimal ET is determined by maximizing the time difference of arrival at the edge of the safety zone between the prey and predator.
source: The optimal ET was determined by maximizing the time difference of arrival at the edge of the safety zone between the prey and predator.
evidence: This describes the optimization criterion used in the model.

claim: The model can clearly explain the observed multiple preferred ETs in fish Pagrus major.
source: By fitting the model to the experimental data of fish Pagrus major, we show that the model can clearly explain the observed multiple preferred ETs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: The model can produce various patterns of ETs empirically observed in other species by changing parameters within a realistic range.
source: By changing the parameters of the same model within a realistic range, we were able to produce various patterns of ETs empirically observed in other species (e.g., insects and frogs): a single preferred ET and multiple preferred ETs at small (20–50°) and large (150–180°) angles from the predator.
evidence: This is a finding based on model simulations with varied parameters.

claim: The escape responses of many invertebrate and lower vertebrate species are controlled by giant neurons that ensure a short response time.
source: The escape responses of many invertebrate and lower vertebrate species are controlled by giant neurons that ensure a short response time (Bullock, 1984).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Flight initiation distance and escape trajectory are fundamental behavioral traits for avoiding predation.
source: Many previous studies have focused on two behavioral traits that are fundamental for avoiding predation: when to escape (i.e., flight initiation distance, which is measured as the distance from the predator at the onset of escape) and where to escape (i.e., escape trajectory [ET], which is measured as the angle of escape direction relative to the stimulus direction) (Cooper, Jr and Blumstein, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Flight initiation distance and escape trajectory largely determine the success or failure of predator evasion.
source: Previous studies have investigated the behavioral and environmental contexts affecting these variables (Meager et al., 2006; Arnott et al., 1999; Bateman and Fleming, 2014; Hein et al., 2018; Broom and Ruxton, 2005; Cooper et al., 2003), because they largely determine the success or failure of predator evasion (Walker et al., 2005; Shifferman and Eilam, 2004; Camhi et al., 1978; Kimura and Kawabata, 2018; Dangles et al., 2006), and hence the fitness of the prey species.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: A large number of models on how animals determine their flight initiation distances have been formulated and tested by experiments.
source: A large number of models on how animals determine their flight initiation distances have been formulated and tested by experiments (Cooper, Jr and Blumstein, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: There are unanswered questions about how the variability of observed ETs is generated.
source: Although a number of models have also been developed to predict animal ETs (Arnott et al., 1999; Weihs and Webb, 1984; Domenici, 2002), there are still some unanswered questions about how the variability of the observed ETs is generated.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge despite existing models.

claim: Two different escape tactics have been proposed to enhance the success of predator evasion: the optimal tactic and the protean tactic.
source: Two different escape tactics (and their combination) have been proposed to enhance the success of predator evasion (Jensen, 2018; Domenici et al., 2011a): the optimal tactic (deterministic), which maximizes the distance between the prey and the predator (Figure 1A; Arnott et al., 1999; Weihs and Webb, 1984; Domenici, 2002; Soto et al., 2015), and the protean tactic (stochastic), which maximizes unpredictability to prevent predators from adjusting their strike trajectories accordingly (Figure 1B; Humphries and Driver, 1970; Jones et al., 2011; Richardson et al., 2018; Moore et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The optimal tactic maximizes the distance between the prey and the predator.
source: the optimal tactic (deterministic), which maximizes the distance between the prey and the predator (Figure 1A; Arnott et al., 1999; Weihs and Webb, 1984; Domenici, 2002; Soto et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The protean tactic maximizes unpredictability to prevent predators from adjusting their strike trajectories.
source: the protean tactic (stochastic), which maximizes unpredictability to prevent predators from adjusting their strike trajectories accordingly (Figure 1B; Humphries and Driver, 1970; Jones et al., 2011; Richardson et al., 2018; Moore et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Previous geometric models predict a single ET that depends on the relative speeds of the predator and the prey.
source: Previous geometric models, which formulate optimal tactics, predict a single ET that depends on the relative speeds of the predator and the prey (Arnott et al., 1999; Weihs and Webb, 1984; Domenici, 2002; Soto et al., 2015), and additionally, predator's turning radii and sensory-motor delay in situations where the predator can adjust its strike path (Howland, 1974; Corcoran and Conner, 2016; Martin et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous models.

claim: The combination of optimal and protean tactics cannot explain the complex ET distributions reported in empirical studies on various taxa.
source: However, the combination of the two tactics cannot explain the complex ET distributions reported in empirical studies on various taxa of invertebrates and lower vertebrates (reviewed in Domenici et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review of empirical studies.

claim: Many animal species show multimodal ETs within a limited angular sector (especially 90–180°).
source: Whereas some animals exhibit unimodal ET patterns that satisfy the prediction of the combined tactics or optimal tactic with behavioral imprecision (e.g., Cooper, 2006), many animal species show multimodal ETs within a limited angular sector (esp., 90–180°) (Figure 1D) (e.g., Arnott et al., 1999; Bateman and Fleming, 2014; Domenici and Blake, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: Some researchers have hypothesized mechanical/sensory constraints to explain the discrepancy between model predictions and empirical data.
source: To explore the discrepancy between the predictions of the models and empirical data, some researchers have hypothesized mechanical/sensory constraints (Domenici et al., 2011a; Domenici et al., 2008); however, the reasons why certain animal species prefer specific multiple ETs remain unclear.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The reasons why certain animal species prefer specific multiple ETs remain unclear.
source: To explore the discrepancy between the predictions of the models and empirical data, some researchers have hypothesized mechanical/sensory constraints (Domenici et al., 2011a; Domenici et al., 2008); however, the reasons why certain animal species prefer specific multiple ETs remain unclear.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current understanding.

claim: Multiple preferred ETs of prey can result from situations in which animals choose one behavior from multiple options.
source: Multiple preferred ETs of prey can result from situations in which animals choose one behavior from multiple options.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation proposed by the authors.

claim: The matching law proposes that the probability of a certain behavior to occur is related to the proportion of rewards obtained.
source: Previous work carried out in the field of human and animal psychology on the choice of a particular behavioral strategy out of a number of options has proposed a principle called 'matching law'. According to this principle, the probability of a certain behavior to occur is related to the proportion of rewards obtained (Reed and Kaplan, 2011; Poling et al., 2011; McDowell, 2013; Houston et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work in psychology.

claim: The matching law contrasts with a purely optimal tactic where animals should always choose the best option.
source: This is in contrast to a purely optimal tactic, where animals should always choose the best option (i.e., the highest rewards obtained) (Houston et al., 2021; Fawcett et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The probability with which a prey chooses a particular ET can be related to the rewards (chances of survival) of each ET option calculated from a predator-prey geometric model.
source: In line with this approach, the probability with which a prey chooses a particular ET can be related to the rewards (chances of survival) of each ET option calculated from a predator-prey geometric model.
evidence: This is a theoretical framework proposed by the authors.

claim: In previous geometric models, the prey was assumed to instantaneously escape in any direction, irrespective of the prey's initial body orientation.
source: In previous geometric models, the prey was assumed to instantaneously escape in any direction, irrespective of the prey's initial body orientation relative to the predator's approach path (hereafter, initial orientation) (Arnott et al., 1999; Weihs and Webb, 1984; Domenici, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous models.

claim: Additional time is required for changing the heading direction (i.e., turn), so the predator can approach the prey while the prey is turning.
source: However, additional time is required for changing the heading direction (i.e., turn); therefore, a realistic model needs to take into account that the predator can approach the prey while the prey is turning (Kimura and Kawabata, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and represents a logical inference about realistic conditions.

claim: In previous models, attacking predators were assumed to move for an infinite distance at a constant speed.
source: Additionally, in previous models, attacking predators were assumed to move for an infinite distance at a constant speed (Arnott et al., 1999; Weihs and Webb, 1984; Domenici, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous models.

claim: The attacks of many real predators, especially ambush ones, end at a certain distance from initial positions of the prey.
source: However, the attacks of many real predators, especially ambush ones, end at a certain distance from initial positions of the prey (Webb and Skadsen, 1980; Fouts and Nelson, 1999; Anderson, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous empirical work.

claim: The authors constructed a geometric model that incorporates the time required for the prey to turn and the endpoint of the predator attack.
source: Therefore, we constructed a geometric model that incorporates two additional factors: the time required for the prey to turn and the endpoint of the predator attack.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach of the study.

claim: The authors tested whether their model could predict empirically observed multimodal ETs using a fish species as a model.
source: First, using a fish species as a model, we tested whether our model could predict empirically observed multimodal ETs.
evidence: This describes a research objective of the study.

claim: The authors investigated how prey fish chose a given ET from multiple options by calculating the chances of survival of each ET option from their model.
source: Second, by calculating the chances of survival of each ET option from our model, we investigated how the prey fish chose a given ET from multiple options.
evidence: This describes a research objective of the study.

claim: The authors tested whether other patterns of empirical ETs could be predicted by extending the model.
source: Third, by extending the model, we tested whether other patterns of empirical ETs could be predicted: unimodal ETs and multimodal ETs directed at small (20–50°) and large (150–180°) angles from the predator's approach direction.
evidence: This describes a research objective of the study.

claim: The authors revised the previous model proposed by Domenici, 2002; Paglianti and Domenici, 2006.
source: We revised the previous model proposed by Domenici, 2002; Paglianti and Domenici, 2006 (Figure 2A) and the model proposed by Corcoran and Conner, 2016 (Appendix 1—figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the methodological approach, referencing previous models and figures.

claim: Other previous models made predictions similar to those of Domenici's model or Corcoran's model, although they used different theoretical approaches.
source: Other previous models (Arnott et al., 1999; Weihs and Webb, 1984; Soto et al., 2015; Martin et al., 2022) made predictions similar to those of Domenici's model or those of Corcoran's model, although they used different theoretical approaches.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous models.

claim: In Domenici's model, the predator with a certain width directly approaches the prey, and the prey should enter the safety zone before the predator reaches that entry point.
source: In Domenici's model, the predator with a certain width (i.e., the width of a killer whale's tail used as a weapon to catch prey) directly approaches the prey, and the prey (the whole body) should enter the safety zone before the predator reaches that entry point.
evidence: This describes the structure of a previous model.

claim: In Domenici's model, the prey can instantaneously escape in any direction, and the predation threat moves linearly and infinitely.
source: In this model, the prey can instantaneously escape in any direction, and the predation threat moves linearly and infinitely.
evidence: This describes assumptions of a previous model.

claim: Corcoran's model includes the concept that the predator can adjust the approach path up to its minimum turning radius.
source: Corcoran's model is based on the same principle as Domenici's model, but includes the concept that the predator (i.e., a bat) can adjust the approach path up to its minimum turning radius.
evidence: This describes a feature of a previous model.

claim: Domenici's model can be regarded as a special case of Corcoran's model when the turning radius of the predator is infinitely large.
source: Thus, Domenici's model can be regarded as a special case of Corcoran's model when the turning radius of the predator is infinitely large.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the relationship between two models.

claim: These models are based on the escape response of the horizontal plane, which is realistic for many fish species as well as terrestrial and benthic species that move on substrates.
source: These models are based on the escape response of the horizontal plane, which is realistic for many fish species as well as terrestrial and benthic species that move on substrates.
evidence: This describes the applicability of the models.

claim: The models can be applied to aerial animals such as moths escaping from bats because many predator-prey interactions are approximately two-dimensional in a local spatial scale.
source: They can also be applied to aerial animals such as moths escaping from bats because many predator-prey interactions are approximately two-dimensional in a local spatial scale (Corcoran and Conner, 2016; Fabian et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The predator does not adjust the strike path during the attack in the experiment with Pagrus major.
source: Hereafter, we explain the modification of Domenici's model (a special case of Corcoran's model) because the data on previously published predator-prey experiments on the same species of prey and predator in our experiment (Kimura and Kawabata, 2018) show that the predator does not adjust the strike path during the attack (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, adjusted angle = 1.0 ± 6.6° [mean ± s.d.], n=5), and thus the number of parameters to estimate can be reduced.
evidence: This is supported by data from a previous study and shown in a figure.

claim: Two factors are added to Domenici's model: the endpoint of the predator attack and the time required for the prey to turn.
source: In our new model (Figure 2B), two factors are added to the previous Domenici's model: the time required for the prey to turn and the endpoint of the predator attack.
evidence: This describes the novel features of the model and is illustrated in Figure 2B.

claim: Most prey species respond to attack by turning at an angle α, and the ET results from the angular sum of α and β.
source: Most prey species respond to the attack by turning at an angle α, and the ET results from the angular sum of α and β.
evidence: This describes the model's representation of prey behavior.

claim: ETs from the left and right sides were pooled and treated as though they were stimulated from the right side.
source: ETs from the left and right sides were pooled and treated as though they were stimulated from the right side (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; see 'Definition of the angles' in Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This describes a methodological decision in data analysis.

claim: The prey can escape from the predator when the time required for the prey to enter the safety zone (Tprey) is shorter than the time required for the predator's capture device to reach that entry point (Tpred).
source: The prey can escape from the predator when the time required for the prey to enter the safety zone (Tprey) is shorter than the time required for the predator's capture device to reach that entry point (Tpred).
evidence: This describes a key assumption of the model.

claim: The prey is assumed to maximize the difference between Tpred and Tprey (Tdiff).
source: Therefore, the prey is assumed to maximize the difference between the Tpred and Tprey (Tdiff).
evidence: This describes the optimization criterion of the model.

claim: The assumption that Tprey is divided into fast-start and constant speed phases is consistent with previous studies.
source: This assumption is consistent with the previous studies (Domenici and Blake, 1991; Danos and Lauder, 2012; Fleuren et al., 2018) and was supported by our experiment (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: Pagrus major exhibited a typical C-start escape response.
source: Pagrus major exhibited a typical C-start escape response (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Figure 3—figure supplement 1), which consists of the initial bend (stage 1), followed by the return tail flip (stage 2), and continuous swimming or coasting (stage 3) (Domenici and Blake, 1997; Weihs, 1973).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by citations and shown in figures.

claim: When the initial orientation was small (0°≤β<30°), two peaks in the ET distribution were observed: a larger peak at around 100° (away response) and a smaller one at around −80° (toward response).
source: When the initial orientation was small (i.e., the prey was attacked head-on; Figure 3A; 0°≤β<30°), two peaks in the ET distribution were observed: a larger peak at around 100° (away response) and a smaller one at around −80° (toward response).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 3A.

claim: As the initial orientation increases (30°≤β<60°), the peak at around −80° disappeared.
source: As the initial orientation increases (Figure 3A; 30°≤β<60°), the peak at around −80° disappeared.
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 3A.

claim: As the initial orientation further increases beyond 60°, another peak appeared at around 170°.
source: As the initial orientation further increases beyond 60°, another peak appeared at around 170° (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 3A.

claim: When the initial orientation was large (150°≤β≤180°), there were two similar-sized peaks in the ET at around 130° (toward response) and 180–200° (away response).
source: When the initial orientation was large (i.e., the prey was attacked from behind; Figure 3A; 150°≤β≤180°), there were two similar-sized peaks in the ET at around 130° (toward response), and 180–200° (away response).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There were significant effects of initial orientation on the ET in both the away and the toward responses.
source: There were significant effects of initial orientation on the ET in both the away and the toward responses (away: generalized additive mixed model [GAMM] F=214.81, p<0.01, n=208; toward: GAMM, F=373.92, p<0.01, n=56).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: There were significant effects of initial orientation on the turn angle α in away and toward responses.
source: There were significant effects of initial orientation on the turn angle α in away and toward responses (Figure 3—figure supplement 2; away: GAMM, F=90.88, p<0.01, n=208; toward: GAMM, F=42.48, p<0.01, n=56).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: In the overall frequency distribution of ETs pooling all data, there were two large peaks at 120–130° and 170–180°, and one small peak at around −80°.
source: In the overall frequency distribution of ETs pooling the data on all initial orientations and both toward and away responses, there were two large peaks at 120–130° and 170–180°, and one small peak at around −80° (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The three peaks in the overall ET distribution were confirmed by the Gaussian mixture model analysis.
source: These three peaks were confirmed by the Gaussian mixture model analysis (Domenici et al., 2008), where we fitted one to nine Gaussian curves to the ETs, and selected the most parsimonious model based on the Akaike information criterion (AIC) (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis result.

claim: There were no significant effects of predator speed on the ET and |α| in either the toward or the away responses.
source: There were no significant effects of predator speed on the ET and |α| in either the toward or the away responses (ET, away: GAMM, F=0.01, p=0.93, n=208; ET, toward: GAMM, F=0.05, P=0.82, n=56; |α|, away: GAMM, F=0.01, p=0.93, n=208; |α|, toward: GAMM, F=0.05, p=0.82, n=56).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: There were no significant effects of predator speed (slow vs. fast) on the variations of ETs and |α| in all 30° initial orientation bins.
source: There were no significant effects of predator speed (slow [from the minimum to the 33.3% quantile]: 0.13–0.93 m s−1; and fast [from the 66.7% quantile to the maximum]: 1.29–1.88 m s−1) on the variations of ETs and |α| in all 30° initial orientation bins (Levene's test, W=0.02–3.22, p=0.09–0.88, n=22–47).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: Dwidth and Rdevice were determined from the mouth shape of the predator when fully opened, which were 18 and 199 mm, respectively.
source: Dwidth and Rdevice were determined from the mouth shape of the predator (the sacrificed specimen for making the dummy predator) when fully opened, which were 18 and 199 mm, respectively.
evidence: This describes how parameter values were measured.

claim: D1, Uprey, and T1(|α|) were directly estimated by analyzing the escape responses of the prey.
source: D1, Uprey, and T1(|α|) were directly estimated by analyzing the escape responses of the prey.
evidence: This describes how parameter values were determined.

claim: Optimal values of Upred and Dattack were determined iteratively by comparing model outputs with observed ETs.
source: Because we have no previous knowledge about the values of Upred and Dattack that the prey regards as dangerous, optimal values of Upred and Dattack were determined iteratively by comparing model outputs with observed ETs.
evidence: This describes the optimization procedure used.

claim: The optimal values of Upred and Dattack were checked with data from previously published predator-prey experiments on the same species.
source: These optimal values were checked afterward with the data from previously published predator-prey experiments on the same species of prey and predator (Kimura and Kawabata, 2018).
evidence: This describes validation of parameter values using previous data.

claim: The optimization procedure was applied to estimating Upred because there was no significant effect of predator speed on ET in the experiment.
source: We applied this optimization procedure to estimating Upred instead of measuring the dummy predator speed per trial in the experiment because there was no significant effect of predator speed on ET in the experiment, suggesting that the prey is likely to have optimized their ETs based on a fixed predator speed (see Discussion for details).
evidence: This explains the rationale for a methodological decision based on experimental results.

claim: The assumption that prey optimize ETs based on a fixed predator speed was supported by follow-up analysis showing worse model fits when using dummy predator speed per trial.
source: This assumption was also supported by the follow-up analysis using the dummy predator speed per trial, where the model fits became worse compared to the model using the fixed predator speed estimated through the optimization procedure (Table 3—source data 1; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from a follow-up analysis.

claim: The distance of the fast-start phase (D1) was regarded as 15 mm based on the relationship between displacement and velocity of the prey in the experiments.
source: The distance of the fast-start phase (D1) was regarded as 15 mm based on the relationship between displacement and velocity of the prey in the experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), where the velocity increased up to about 15 mm of displacement from the initial position, beyond which it plateaus
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: Over the 15 mm displacement from the initial position, there were no significant differences in the mean velocity between any combinations of 3 mm intervals in any 30° |α| bins.
source: over the 15 mm displacement from the initial position, there were no significant differences in the mean velocity between any combinations of 3 mm intervals in any 30° |α| bins (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; paired t-test with Bonferroni's correction, all p=1.00, n=23).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: There were significant effects of |α| on the time for a displacement of 15 mm from the initial position.
source: There were significant effects of |α| on the time for a displacement of 15 mm from the initial position (GAMM, F=78.84, p<0.01, n=263; note that the sample size is smaller than the total number of observations, 264, because the prey did not move over 15 mm in one case)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: There were significant effects of |α| on the mean velocity during the displacement of 0-15 mm.
source: and on the mean velocity during the displacement (GAMM, F=76.00, p<0.01, n=263).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: There were no significant effects of |α| on the time required for a displacement of 15–30 mm from the initial position.
source: However, there were no significant effects of |α| on the time required for a displacement of 15–30 mm from the initial position (GAMM, F=1.52, p=0.22, n=257; note that the sample size is smaller than the total number of observations, 264, because the prey did not move over 30 mm in seven cases)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: There were no significant effects of |α| on the mean velocity during the displacement of 15-30 mm.
source: and on the mean velocity during the displacement (GAMM, F=0.89, p=0.27, n=257).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: The mean velocity of the prey during the constant phase Uprey was estimated to be 1.04 m s–1.
source: Therefore, the time required for the prey to turn was incorporated into the model by analyzing the relationship between |α| and the time required for a displacement of 15 mm. The mean velocity of the prey during the constant phase Uprey was estimated to be 1.04 m s–1, based on the experimental data.
evidence: This is a parameter value estimated from experimental data.

claim: The overall results of the study are insensitive to changes in the cut-off distance (10, 15, or 20 mm).
source: Because the cut-off distance might affect the overall results of the study, we have repeated all the statistical analyses (see Tables 2 and 3, and the text below for results with a cut-off distance of 15 mm) with cut-off distances of 10 and 20 mm and confirmed that the overall results are insensitive to the changes (Table 2—source data 1; Table 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is a result from sensitivity analysis.

claim: The time required for a displacement of 15 mm was constant up to 44° of |α|, above which the time linearly increased in response to the increase of |α|.
source: The relationship between |α| and the time required for a displacement of 15 mm, T1(|α|), is shown in Figure 4. The time was constant up to 44° of |α|, above which the time linearly increased in response to the increase of |α| (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In the hierarchical Bayesian model for T1(|α|), the lowest WAIC was obtained for the piecewise linear regression model.
source: In the hierarchical Bayesian model, the lowest widely applicable or Watanabe-Akaike information criterion (WAIC) was obtained for the piecewise linear regression model (Table 2).
evidence: This is a statistical result from model comparison.

claim: In the hierarchical Bayesian model for initial velocity after stage 1 turn, the lowest WAIC was obtained for the piecewise linear regression model.
source: In the hierarchical Bayesian model, the lowest WAIC was obtained for the piecewise linear regression model (Table 2).
evidence: This is a statistical result from model comparison.

claim: The change points of the two relationships (T1(|α|) and initial velocity) were not significantly different.
source: In both relationships, the regression lines by the piecewise linear model were similar to those by the GAMM, suggesting that the general trends of the relationships were clearly captured by this method. The change points of the two relationships were not significantly different (difference: 1.70±18.01° [mean ± 95% Bayesian credible intervals]).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis.

claim: Fish with a small |α| (<<45°) can accomplish the stage 1 turn quickly but their velocity after the turn is lower.
source: These results indicate that fish with a small |α| (<<45°) can accomplish the stage 1 turn quickly but their velocity after the turn is lower, while fish with an intermediate |α| (=45°) spend a longer time on the stage 1 turn, but their velocity after the turn is higher.
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental results.

claim: Fish with an intermediate |α| (=45°) spend a longer time on the stage 1 turn, but their velocity after the turn is higher.
source: These results indicate that fish with a small |α| (<<45°) can accomplish the stage 1 turn quickly but their velocity after the turn is lower, while fish with an intermediate |α| (=45°) spend a longer time on the stage 1 turn, but their velocity after the turn is higher.
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental results.

claim: Fish with a large |α| (>>45°) spend a still longer time on the stage 1 turn, but their velocity after the turn is similar to that with an intermediate |α|.
source: Fish with a large |α| (>>45°) spend a still longer time on the stage 1 turn, but their velocity after the turn is similar to that with an intermediate |α| (Figure 4).
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental results shown in Figure 4.

claim: The optimal value of Dattack is 34.73 mm and the optimal value of Upred is 1.54 m s–1.
source: The result shows that the optimal value of Dattack is 34.73 mm and the optimal value of Upred is 1.54 m s–1.
evidence: This is a result from the optimization procedure.

claim: The estimated Dattack value is at the upper limit of the empirical data from previous predator-prey experiments.
source: Using data from previously published predator-prey experiments on the same species of prey and predator (Kimura and Kawabata, 2018), we show that the estimated Dattack value is at the upper limit of the empirical data and the estimated Upred value is higher than the mean of the observed predator speed (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous data shown in a figure.

claim: The estimated Upred value is higher than the mean of the observed predator speed in previous experiments.
source: Using data from previously published predator-prey experiments on the same species of prey and predator (Kimura and Kawabata, 2018), we show that the estimated Dattack value is at the upper limit of the empirical data and the estimated Upred value is higher than the mean of the observed predator speed (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous data shown in a figure.

claim: The estimated Upred value is higher than the mean of the observed dummy predator speed in the current experiment.
source: Similarly, the estimated Upred value is higher than the mean of the observed dummy predator speed in our experiment (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C, D).
evidence: This is a comparison with experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: The values independently estimated in the present study are reasonable, and the prey may choose ETs by overestimating the values of Dattack and Upred.
source: These results suggest that the values independently estimated in the present study are reasonable, and the prey may choose ETs by overestimating the values of Dattack and Upred.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the comparison between estimated and observed values.

claim: The model predicts a multimodal pattern of ET with a higher peak at the maximum Tdiff and a second lower peak at the second local maximum of Tdiff.
source: In general, the predicted ETs are in line with the observed ones, where the model predicts a multimodal pattern of ET with a higher peak (i.e., optimal ET) at the maximum Tdiff (Tdiff,1) and a second lower peak (i.e., suboptimal ET) at the second local maximum of Tdiff (Tdiff,2).
evidence: This describes the model predictions.

claim: 41%, 76%, and 94% of observed ETs were within the top 10%, 25%, and 40% quantiles, respectively, of the theoretical ETs.
source: Forty-one percent, 76%, and 94% of observed ETs were within the top 10%, 25%, and 40% quantiles, respectively (0.1, 0.25, 0.40 ranking index) of the theoretical ETs (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between model predictions and observations.

claim: When the initial orientation is <20°, the optimal and suboptimal ETs are around 100° (away response) and −100° (toward response), respectively, which is consistent with the bimodal distribution in the experiment.
source: When the initial orientation is <20° (Figure 5A; β=15°, Figures 5B and 6B), the optimal and suboptimal ETs are around 100° (away response) and −100° (toward response), respectively, which is consistent with the bimodal distribution of our experiment (Figure 3A; 0°≤β<30°).
evidence: This compares model predictions with experimental observations shown in figures.

claim: At initial orientations in the range 20‒60°, the suboptimal ET switches from around −100° to 170°.
source: At initial orientations in the range 20‒60°, the suboptimal ET switches from around −100° to 170° (Figure 5A; β=45°, Figures 5B and 6B), although Tdiff,2 is extremely small compared to Tdiff,1 (Figure 5A; β=45°, Figures 5B and 6B).
evidence: This describes model predictions shown in figures.

claim: When the initial orientation is 60‒120°, the optimal ET is 100‒140° (gradually shifting from 100° to 140°), and the suboptimal ET is around 170°.
source: When the initial orientation is 60‒120° (Figure 5A; β=75° and β=105°, Figures 5B and 6B), the optimal ET is 100‒140° (gradually shifting from 100° to 140°), and the suboptimal ET is around 170°. These two peaks and the shift of the optimal ET are consistent with the experimental results (Figure 3A; 60°≤β<90° and 90°≤β<120°).
evidence: This compares model predictions with experimental observations shown in figures.

claim: The values of the optimal and suboptimal ETs are reversed at initial orientations > 120°.
source: The values of the optimal and suboptimal ETs are reversed at initial orientations > 120° (Figures 5B and 6B), as the optimal and suboptimal values become 170‒180° and around 140°, respectively (Figure 5A). These results are again consistent with the bimodal distribution of our experiments (Figure 3A; 120°≤β<150° and 150°≤β≤180°).
evidence: This compares model predictions with experimental observations shown in figures.

claim: The theoretical ET distribution estimated by Monte Carlo simulation shows two large peaks at around 110–130° and 170–180°, and one small peak at around −100°.
source: Figure 5C shows the circular histogram of the overall theoretical ETs estimated by Monte Carlo simulation. The theoretical ETs show two large peaks at around 110–130° and 170–180°, and one small peak at around −100° (Figure 5C).
evidence: This describes simulation results shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The theoretically estimated ET distribution is similar to the frequency distribution of the observed ETs.
source: This theoretically estimated ET distribution is similar to the frequency distribution of the observed ETs (Figure 3C); there were no significant differences in the frequency distribution between theoretical ETs (n=264 per simulation) and observed ETs (n=264) in 971 of 1000 simulations (Table 3; two-sample Kuiper test, median V=0.11, median p=0.44).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison between simulations and observations.

claim: The fish chose the optimal and suboptimal ETs to a similar extent when the optimal ET advantage is negligible.
source: The fish chose the optimal and suboptimal ETs to a similar extent when the optimal ET advantage is negligible (Figure 6C). For example, when looking at the optimal ET advantage <2 ms, where the initial orientation is 0‒7° and 106–180° (46% of all initial orientations), the proportion of the optimal ET used was only 55% (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is an analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The proportion of the optimal ET used was 81% when the optimal ET advantage is higher than 6 ms.
source: On the other hand, the proportion of the optimal ET used was 81% when the optimal ET advantage is higher than 6 ms (i.e., when the initial orientation is 21–75°) (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is an analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: There was a significant effect of optimal ET advantage on the proportion of the optimal ET used by fish.
source: There was a significant effect of optimal ET advantage on the proportion of the optimal ET used by fish tested in our experiments (mixed-effects logistic regression analysis, χ2=10.72, p<0.01, n=247).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis.

claim: In all three additional geometric models (with only Dattack, with only T1(|α|), and the null model), the theoretical ET distributions were significantly different from the observed ET distributions.
source: To investigate the effects of two factors (i.e., the endpoint of the predator attack Dattack and the time required for the prey to turn T1(|α|)) on the predictions of ET separately, we constructed three additional geometric models (Figure 5—figure supplements 4–6): a model that includes only Dattack, a model that includes only T1(|α|), and a null model that includes neither factors (Figure 2A and Domenici, 2002). In all of these models, the theoretical ET distributions estimated through Monte Carlo simulations were significantly different from the observed ET distributions (Table 3; two-sample Kuiper test, median p<0.01).
evidence: This is a result from model comparison shown in figures and table.

claim: The model with Dattack and the model with T1(|α|) show multimodal patterns of ET distribution, but the simulations do not match the experimental data.
source: Although the model with Dattack and the model with T1(|α|) show multimodal patterns of ET distribution, the simulation based on these models do not match the experimental data, likely because of differences in the values and relative heights of the peaks (Figure 5—figure supplements 4 and 5).
evidence: This is a result from model comparison shown in figures.

claim: The null model shows a unimodal pattern of ET distribution.
source: The null model shows a unimodal pattern of ET distribution (Figure 5—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is a result from model simulation shown in a figure.

claim: Some animals show different patterns of ETs: a single preferred ET either at around 180° or at around 90°, and multiple preferred ETs at small and large angles from the predator's approach direction.
source: Although many fish species and animals from other taxa exhibit multiple preferred ETs similar to what we observed here, some animals show different patterns of ETs: for example, a single preferred ET either at around 180° (Kanou et al., 1999) or at around 90° (Cooper, 2006), and multiple preferred ETs at small and large angles from the predator's approach direction (Fuiman, 1993; Martín and López, 1996; Bulbert et al., 2015; Figure 7A–C).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: At small Upred, the model predicts one strong peak at around 180°.
source: At small Upred, the model predicts one strong peak at around 180° (Figure 7D), whereas at large Upred, the model predicts a strong peak at around 90° (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is a result from model simulation shown in Figure 7D.

claim: At large Upred, the model predicts a strong peak at around 90°.
source: At small Upred, the model predicts one strong peak at around 180° (Figure 7D), whereas at large Upred, the model predicts a strong peak at around 90° (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is a result from model simulation shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The model where the predator can adjust the approach path and its attack lasts for a long distance predicts multiple preferred ETs directed at small (at around 30°) and large (at around 170°) angles from the predator's approach direction.
source: The model where the predator can adjust the approach path and its attack lasts for a long distance (i.e., large Dattack) predicts multiple preferred ETs directed at small (at around 30°) and large (at around 170°) angles from the predator's approach direction (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is a result from model simulation shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The model has the potential to explain various patterns of observed animal ETs.
source: These results indicate that our model has the potential to explain various patterns of observed animal ETs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: The geometric model incorporating Dattack and T1(|α|) clearly explains the multimodal patterns of ETs in P. major.
source: Our geometric model, incorporating the endpoint of the predator attack, Dattack, and the time required for the prey to turn, T1(|α|), to maximize the difference between the prey and the predator in the time of arrival at the edge of the safety zone, Tdiff, clearly explains the multimodal patterns of ETs in P. major.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on model-data comparison.

claim: The multimodal patterns of ETs are likely attributable to the existence of two escape routes: either moving sideways to depart from the predator's strike path or moving opposite to the predator's direction to outrun it.
source: Specifically, according to the model, when the prey escapes at 140° or 170°, it will not be captured by the predator. On the other hand, when the prey escapes along an intermediate trajectory (157°), it will be captured because it swims toward the corner of the danger zone to exit it, and therefore it needs to travel a longer distance than when escaping at 140° or 170°. This example illustrates that the multimodal patterns of ETs are likely to be attributable to the existence of two escape routes: either moving sideways to depart from the predator's strike path or moving opposite to the predator's direction to outrun it.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model results illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: Both components of the predator-prey interaction (Dattack and T1(|α|)) added to the previous model are important for accurate predictions of the ET distribution.
source: Interestingly, both components of the predator-prey interaction (i.e., Dattack and T1(|α|)) added to the previous model (Domenici, 2002) are important for accurate predictions of the ET distribution because when they are considered by the model separately, the predictions do not match the experimental data (Figure 5—figure supplements 4 and 5; Table 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on model comparison results.

claim: The prey combines optimal and protean tactics by using multiple preferred ETs.
source: Our results suggest that the prey combines these two different tactics by using multiple preferred ETs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results.

claim: When the optimal ET advantage is large (initial orientation 20–60°), the prey mainly uses the optimal ET.
source: Specifically, when the optimal ET advantage is large (i.e., when the initial orientation is 20–60°), the prey mainly uses the optimal ET (Figures 3A and 6).
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental results shown in figures.

claim: When the optimal ET advantage over the suboptimal ET is negligible (initial orientation close to 0° or within 110‒180°), the prey uses optimal and suboptimal ETs to a similar extent.
source: However, when the optimal ET advantage over the suboptimal ET is negligible (i.e., the initial orientation is close to 0° or within the range 110‒180°), the prey uses optimal and suboptimal ETs to a similar extent (Figures 3A and 6).
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental results shown in figures.

claim: When the optimal ET advantage is negligible, the ET of the prey would be highly unpredictable for the predator.
source: In such cases, the ET of the prey would be highly unpredictable for the predator.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the observation that prey use multiple ETs with similar frequency.

claim: The unpredictability at initial orientations near 0° and 180° is consistent with the study that applied the conventional geometric model to larval zebrafish.
source: The unpredictability at initial orientations near 0° and 180° is consistent with the study that applied the conventional geometric model to the larval zebrafish Danio rerio (Nair et al., 2017), where the optimal and suboptimal ETs are approximately symmetrical to the axis of the predator attack.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The unpredictability at initial orientations near 0° and 180° can be explained by the toward-away indecision at orientations nearly perpendicular to the threat.
source: This phenomenon can be explained by the toward-away indecision at orientations nearly perpendicular to the threat (Domenici and Blake, 1993; Domenici and Batty, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The unpredictability observed at initial orientations near 110–180° is related to the similarly advantageous choice between escaping with an ET at around 140° or 180°.
source: On the other hand, the unpredictability observed at initial orientations near 110–180° is related to the similarly advantageous choice between escaping with an ET at around 140° or 180°.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results.

claim: At initial orientations >120°, the two ETs (around 140° and 180°) are reached by using toward and away responses, respectively.
source: Interestingly, at initial orientations >120°, our results show that these two ETs are reached by using toward and away responses, respectively.
evidence: This is an observation from the results.

claim: The overlap between the ETs of toward and away responses suggests that toward responses are not 'tactical mistakes' but are related to reaching an optimal or suboptimal ET.
source: The overlap between the ETs of toward and away responses in the overall dataset (Figure 3) suggests that toward responses are not 'tactical mistakes' of the prey that turns toward a threat, but are simply related to reaching an optimal or suboptimal ET.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results shown in Figure 3.

claim: The prey strategically adjusts the use of optimal and protean tactics based on their initial orientation.
source: These results suggest that the prey strategically adjusts the use of optimal and protean tactics based on their initial orientation. This allows the prey to have unpredictable ETs, thereby preventing predators from anticipating their escape behavior, while keeping Tdiff large enough to enter the safety zone before the predator reaches it.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results.

claim: The prey follows the matching law, where the probability that an optimal or suboptimal ET is chosen is proportional to its chances of survival.
source: From a behavioral decision-making perspective, our results suggest that the prey follows the matching law (Reed and Kaplan, 2011; Poling et al., 2011; McDowell, 2013; Houston et al., 2021), where the probability that an optimal or suboptimal ET is chosen is proportional to its chances of survival (i.e., Tdiff).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results supported by citations.

claim: The prey stochastically draws from a Bernoulli distribution dictated by the optimal ET advantage for the binary choice between an optimal and a suboptimal ET.
source: As the matching law predicts (Houston et al., 2021), the prey stochastically draws from a Bernoulli distribution dictated by the optimal ET advantage for the binary choice between an optimal and a suboptimal ET, thereby introducing an element of unpredictability, which can prevent predators from learning.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results supported by a citation.

claim: Most empirical studies supporting the matching law use unnatural reinforcement learning paradigms or human behaviors.
source: Because most empirical studies supporting the matching law use unnatural reinforcement learning paradigms or human behaviors (Reed and Kaplan, 2011; Poling et al., 2011; McDowell, 2013; Houston et al., 2021), this result suggests that the matching law is also applicable to animal behavior in realistic contexts.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The matching law is applicable to animal behavior in realistic contexts.
source: Because most empirical studies supporting the matching law use unnatural reinforcement learning paradigms or human behaviors (Reed and Kaplan, 2011; Poling et al., 2011; McDowell, 2013; Houston et al., 2021), this result suggests that the matching law is also applicable to animal behavior in realistic contexts.
evidence: This is an inference from the current results and previous work.

claim: The initial orientation of the prey has been incorporated into various neural circuit models.
source: The initial orientation of the prey has been incorporated into various neural circuit models (Eaton et al., 2001; Yono and Shimozawa, 2008; Card, 2012; Levi and Camhi, 2000), but these models assume that prey animals always escape in a 180° direction (i.e., opposite to the stimulus source), irrespective of the initial orientation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Previous neural circuit models assume that prey animals always escape in a 180° direction, irrespective of the initial orientation.
source: The initial orientation of the prey has been incorporated into various neural circuit models (Eaton et al., 2001; Yono and Shimozawa, 2008; Card, 2012; Levi and Camhi, 2000), but these models assume that prey animals always escape in a 180° direction (i.e., opposite to the stimulus source), irrespective of the initial orientation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The present study shows that animals use suboptimal ETs as well as optimal ETs, and that these ETs may change in a nonlinear fashion, depending on the initial orientation.
source: However, the present study shows that animals use suboptimal ETs as well as optimal ETs, and that these ETs may change in a nonlinear fashion, depending on the initial orientation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: The Mauthner cell and other neurons involved may be activated in accordance with the Bernoulli probabilities dictated by the model.
source: More specifically, the Mauthner cell and other neurons involved may be activated in accordance with the Bernoulli probabilities dictated by the model, which determine the proportions of away and toward responses and the magnitude of turn to achieve the multiple preferred ETs.
evidence: This is a speculation about neural mechanisms based on the model.

claim: New neurophysiological models of ETs are required to understand how neural circuits process sensory cues resulting in multiple preferred ETs.
source: Thus, we require new neurophysiological models of ETs to understand how neural circuits process the sensory cues of a threatening stimulus, resulting in muscle actions that generate multiple preferred ETs.
evidence: This is a conclusion about future research needs.

claim: The geometric model assumes that the prey determines the ETs based on a fixed predator speed.
source: Our geometric model assumes that the prey determines the ETs based on a fixed predator speed. This assumption is supported by the results of our experiments, where the effects of predator speed on the mean and variability of ETs are not significant.
evidence: This describes a model assumption supported by experimental results.

claim: It is possible that a predator speed outside the range used in the experiment may affect ETs.
source: Although we did not find any effect of predator speed, it is possible that a speed outside the range we used may affect ETs.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the study.

claim: Larval zebrafish exhibit less variable ETs under faster threats than they do under slower threats.
source: Recent studies show that larval zebrafish exhibit less variable ETs under faster threats than they do under slower threats (Stewart et al., 2014; Bhattacharyya et al., 2017), and the difference in ET variability between fast and slow threats is dependent on whether the Mauthner cell is active or not (Bhattacharyya et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The difference in ET variability between fast and slow threats in zebrafish is dependent on whether the Mauthner cell is active or not.
source: Recent studies show that larval zebrafish exhibit less variable ETs under faster threats than they do under slower threats (Stewart et al., 2014; Bhattacharyya et al., 2017), and the difference in ET variability between fast and slow threats is dependent on whether the Mauthner cell is active or not (Bhattacharyya et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Differences in ET variability compared to previous studies could be related to the different involvement of the Mauthner cells.
source: Therefore, any differences in the ET variability of the present study compared to previous studies could be related to the different involvement of the Mauthner cells.
evidence: This is a speculation based on previous work.

claim: The choice of ET only matters to a prey when the predator speed is intermediate.
source: Using the conventional geometric model (Weihs and Webb, 1984), Soto et al. showed that the choice of ET only matters to a prey when the predator speed is intermediate, because a prey that is much faster than its predator can escape by a broad range of ETs, whereas a prey that is much slower than its predator cannot escape by any ETs (Soto et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The predator speed used in this study is in the range of the real predator speed in the previous study using the same species.
source: The predator speed used in this study is in the range of the real predator speed in the previous study using the same species of both predator and prey (Kimura and Kawabata, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The results are ecologically relevant, and the prey is likely to have optimized their ETs based on a fixed predator speed.
source: Thus, our results are ecologically relevant, and the prey is likely to have optimized their ETs based on a fixed predator speed, where the choice of ET strongly affects their survival.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results.

claim: The time required for a 15 mm displacement is relatively constant up to an |α| of about 45°, while a further change in |α| requires additional time.
source: The relationship between |α| and the time required for a 15 mm displacement, T1(|α|), (Figure 4A) indicates that the time required for a 15 mm displacement is relatively constant up to an |α| of about 45°, while a further change in |α| requires additional time.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The relationship between |α| and T1(|α|) is likely attributable to the kinematics and hydrodynamics of the C-start escape response.
source: This relationship is likely to be attributable to the kinematics and hydrodynamics of the C-start escape response, because the initial velocity after the stage 1 turn increases linearly up to about 45°, beyond which it plateaus (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A recent study on swimming efficiency during acceleration found that efficiency increases linearly with yaw amplitudes up to a certain value, beyond which efficiency plateaus.
source: Interestingly, a recent study on swimming efficiency during acceleration found that efficiency increases linearly with yaw amplitudes up to a certain value, beyond which efficiency plateaus (Akanyeti et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The empirical data are obtained from one species of hatchery-reared fish with a specific life stage, which has never experienced predators.
source: Based on the STRANGE framework for animal behavior research (Webster and Rutz, 2020), we identified potential biases that may limit the generalizability of our findings. Our empirical data are obtained from one species of hatchery-reared fish with a specific life stage, which has never experienced predators.
evidence: This describes the study sample and acknowledges potential limitations.

claim: This study alone cannot exclude the possibility that fish of different species, origins, life stages, and rearing histories have different rules for ETs.
source: Therefore, this study alone cannot exclude the possibility that fish of different species, origins, life stages, and rearing histories have different rules for ETs, which our model cannot explain.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the study.

claim: Similar multiple preferred ETs have been observed in many fish species and other animal taxa, including hatcheries/wild origins and different life stages.
source: However, similar multiple preferred ETs have been observed in many fish species and other animal taxa, including hatcheries/wild origins and different life stages (Domenici et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review.

claim: The model is not specific to the experiment but is applicable to other cases showing multiple preferred ETs.
source: Therefore, we believe that our model is not specific to our experiment but is applicable to other cases showing multiple preferred ETs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison with previous work.

claim: Based on the model assuming that the predator makes an in-line attack, either single or multiple ETs at around 90–150° and around 180° are predicted.
source: Based on the model assuming that the predator makes an in-line attack toward the prey, which is realistic for ambush and stalk-and-attack predators (Moore and Biewener, 2015) (e.g., frogs [Camhi et al., 1978], spiders [Dangles et al., 2006], and fish [Kimura and Kawabata, 2018; Webb and Skadsen, 1980; Fouts and Nelson, 1999; Rand and Lauder, 1981]), either single or multiple ETs at around 90–150° and around 180° are predicted, as have been observed in many empirical studies of animals escaping from ambush predators and artificial stimuli (Domenici et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Based on the model assuming that the predator can adjust its approach path, multiple ETs directed at small and large angles from the predator's approach direction can be predicted.
source: Based on the model assuming that the predator can adjust its approach path, which is realistic for pursuit predators, multiple ETs directed at small and large angles from the predator's approach direction can be predicted, as observed in the empirical studies of prey escaping from pursuit predators (Corcoran and Conner, 2016; Bulbert et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The work represents a major advancement in understanding the basis of the variability in ETs observed in previous works.
source: Our work represents a major advancement in understanding the basis of the variability in ETs observed in previous works (reviewed in Domenici et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is a claim about the significance of the work.

claim: Prey use multiple preferred ETs to maximize the time difference between themselves and the attacking predator, while keeping a high level of unpredictability.
source: Our results suggest that prey use multiple preferred ETs to maximize the time difference between themselves and the attacking predator, while keeping a high level of unpredictability.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the results.

claim: Multimodal ETs similar to what was observed have been found in many fish species and other animal taxa.
source: Because multimodal ETs similar to what we observed here have been found in many fish species and other animal taxa (Domenici et al., 2011b), this behavioral phenotype may result from convergent evolution in phylogenetically distant animals.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review.

claim: The multimodal ET behavioral phenotype may result from convergent evolution in phylogenetically distant animals.
source: Because multimodal ETs similar to what we observed here have been found in many fish species and other animal taxa (Domenici et al., 2011b), this behavioral phenotype may result from convergent evolution in phylogenetically distant animals.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the widespread occurrence of the behavior.

claim: The findings open new avenues to investigate how animals determine their ETs from multiple options with specific probabilities modulated by initial orientation.
source: From a neurosensory perspective, our findings open new avenues to investigate how the animals determine their ETs from multiple options with specific probabilities, which are modulated by the initial orientation with respect to the threat.
evidence: This is a conclusion about future research directions.

claim: Initial orientation ranges from 0° (when the prey is attacked from front) to 180° (when the prey is attacked from behind).
source: Initial orientation (β): the angle between the line passing through the prey's CoM (located at 34% of the total length from the tip of the snout; Kimura and Kawabata, 2018) and the tip of the snout at the onset of stage 1, and the midline of the predator model attacking in a straight line. Initial orientation ranges from 0° (i.e., when the prey is attacked from front) to 180° (i.e., when the prey is attacked from behind).
evidence: This defines a methodological term.

claim: The away and toward responses were defined by the first detectable movement of the fish in a direction either away from or toward the predator, respectively.
source: Directionality: the away and toward responses were defined by the first detectable movement of the fish in a direction either away from or toward the predator, respectively (Domenici et al., 2011b).
evidence: This defines a methodological term supported by a citation.

claim: The angles of the away and toward responses are assigned positive and negative values, respectively.
source: Turn angle (α): the angle between the line passing through the CoM and the tip of the snout at the onset of stage 1, and the line passing through the CoM at the onset of stage 1 and the CoM at the end of stage 2. The angles of the away and toward responses are assigned positive and negative values, respectively.
evidence: This defines a methodological convention.

claim: The experimental data exhibited no asymmetry in directionality.
source: Because the experimental data exhibited no asymmetry in directionality (Fisher's exact test, p=1.00, n=264) and ET distribution (two-sample Kuiper test, V=0.14, p=0.61, n=264), we pooled the ETs from the left and right sides, treating all fish as though they were attacked from the right side (Domenici et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is a statistical result justifying a methodological decision.

claim: The experimental data exhibited no asymmetry in ET distribution.
source: Because the experimental data exhibited no asymmetry in directionality (Fisher's exact test, p=1.00, n=264) and ET distribution (two-sample Kuiper test, V=0.14, p=0.61, n=264), we pooled the ETs from the left and right sides, treating all fish as though they were attacked from the right side (Domenici et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is a statistical result justifying a methodological decision.

claim: Sixty-five individuals of Pagrus major were purchased from commercial hatcheries.
source: Sixty-five individuals were purchased from commercial hatcheries (Marua Suisan Co., Ltd., Ehime, Japan), where they were reared communally in artificial tanks.
evidence: This describes the sample source.

claim: The sex of the fish was not determined because the species of this size is in a bisexual juvenile stage.
source: The sex of the fish was not determined because the species of this size is in a bisexual juvenile stage (Law and Sadovy de Mitcheson, 2017).
evidence: This explains a methodological decision supported by a citation.

claim: The value of Fulton's condition factor suggests that all fish were in a good nutritious condition.
source: The value of Fulton's condition factor (30.64±2.43 [26.10–35.56], mean ± s.d. [range]), calculated by the body weight of the fish divided by the standard length cubed, suggests that all fish were in a good nutritious condition (Miyajima-taga et al., 2014; Kudoh et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an interpretation of a measurement supported by citations.

claim: There should be no bias in selecting individuals with specific behavioral types because it was not difficult to capture any individual by a hand net.
source: Because it was not difficult to capture any individual by a hand net, there should be no bias in selecting individuals with specific behavioral types.
evidence: This is a methodological consideration.

claim: The dummy predator was a cast of Sebastiscus marmoratus (164 mm in total length and 36 mm in mouth width).
source: After the acclimation period, the PVC pipe was slowly removed, and the dummy predator, a cast of Sebastiscus marmoratus (164 mm in total length and 36 mm in mouth width), was moved toward the P. major for a distance of 200 mm (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This describes the experimental setup.

claim: Sebastiscus marmoratus attacks Pagrus major using a variable speed (1.10±0.65 [0.09–2.31] m s−1).
source: Because the previous work shows that S. marmoratus attacks P. major using a variable speed (1.10±0.65 [0.09–2.31] m s−1, mean ± s.d. [range]) (Kimura and Kawabata, 2018), we used various strengths of plastic rubber bands to investigate the effect of predator speed on ET.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Each individual Pagrus major was stimulated from 5 to 23 times with a time interval of at least 15 min.
source: Each individual P. major was stimulated from 5 to 23 times with a time interval of at least 15 min, and, in total, 297 trials were conducted.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: 33 trials were eliminated from the analysis because P. major moved away from the striking course of the dummy predator before the stimulation (14 trials) or because bubbles obscured the P. major image (19 trials).
source: We eliminated 33 trials from the analysis because P. major moved away from the striking course of the dummy predator before the stimulation (in 14 trials) and because bubbles obscured the P. major image (in 19 trials).
evidence: This describes data exclusion criteria.

claim: The final data analyzed are 5–20 escape responses per individual and, in total, 264 escape responses.
source: The final data analyzed are 5–20 escape responses per individual and, in total, 264 escape responses.
evidence: This describes the final sample size.

claim: The animal care and experimental procedures were approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee of the Faculty of Fisheries, Nagasaki University.
source: The animal care and experimental procedures were approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee of the Faculty of Fisheries (Permit No. NF-0002), Nagasaki University in accordance with the Guidelines for Animal Experimentation of the Faculty of Fisheries and the Regulations of the Animal Care and Use Committee, Nagasaki University.
evidence: This describes ethical approval.
